#2718. Fantasy Football Week 11 RB Report: Another fumble makes D'Andre Swift tough to trust, plus more backfield splits

Let's take a second to appreciate the backup running back and the importance of having that insurance on your bench. Emmett Johnson drew another start in place of the injured Kenneth Walker III on Sunday. For the third time in four weeks, the rookie back went for 22+ fantasy points on a hefty 23 carries for 105 yards and a score, plus four catches for 38 yards. Most of that damage was done well before the game clock wound down in the fourth quarter.

If you're a Walker manager who was smart enough to add Johnson back after Week 8, nice work. If you were like me (in one league) and didn't grab Johnson to replace Walker, well … it's been a rough watch the past month or so.

In this piece, we talk a lot about backfield splits and depth running backs, specifically, in an attempt to inform you for future weeks. Let's see what the highlights and box scores show us that we can use for fantasy football going into Week 12 and the Thanksgiving week slate.

It was an ugly week in general for the Bears offense in a spot we thought could produce points, considering the team had an implied total around 30. Instead, we got inconsistency, particularly in the run game despite the return of Kyle Monangai. He had missed the past five games due to turf toe and a thumb injury. This was also an elite matchup for running backs; New Orleans entered Week 11 allowing the sixth-most rushing yards per game and sixth-most rushing TDs this season.

While Swift got to an OK floor for fantasy purposes because of a short TD catch, he could be back in the doghouse after another lost fumble, his third of the season. As a result, we saw carries for fourth-string RB Salvon Ahmed, with Roschon Johnson leaving the game early due to an ankle injury. Monangai also wasn't his usual efficient self, though we're willing to give him a pass coming back after a long absence.

Let's talk about Swift first. In games following a Swift fumble, Swift maintained a heavy workload with 22 touches in Week 3 and 13 in Week 5 (no Caleb Williams). So Swift shouldn't lose his role, but he also hasn't been all that impressive. He doesn't have a carry longer than 15 yards since Week 1 and doesn't have a catch that went for more than 13 yards since Week 2. Ben Johnson could opt to lean more on Monangai, but he and Swift have had a relatively even split of the carries when both are healthy, with Swift being more of a threat in the passing game. Ahmed also didn't look all that bad and could leech a few touches.

The next two weeks aren't ideal, either. The Bears get the Lions on Thanksgiving on the road and the Jaguars in Week 13, two of the worst matchups for RBs in fantasy. It will be tough to count on both Swift and Monangai as anything more than flex options in the short term, and after that we could see the latter take on more work if he can stay healthy. The matchups soften a bit in a key stretch from Weeks 14-16.

Maybe it was the Panthers defense but the Ravens offense looks revived with Jacoby Brissett under center. At least for fantasy purposes. Baltimore scored 33 points and had over 400 yards of offense Sunday in the narrow loss to Carolina. For real life, it was brutal. For fantasy managers, it was a sigh of relief for those with Henry and Zay Flowers.

But we're here to talk about the backfield specifically, where Henry got back to work with his highest total on the ground since Week 5, when he went for over 100 yards rushing. He now has four total TDs in the past three games and a useful nine catches in the past two. A lost fumble put a minor dent in his final total as well.

Despite getting back on track the past two weeks, at least from a fantasy points perspective, there's still cause for concern for Henry managers. And it's in the form of Hill.

The backup RB put together another strong outing, nearly reaching 100 total yards on just 10 touches with a 19-yard TD before halftime. Hill also had a 36-yard long rush in the game that resulted in a fumble just before scoring. All in all, he continues to showcase big-play ability. He entered the game averaging 6.8 yards per carry and had 11.5 per against the Panthers. That's going to keep Hill involved.

Looking ahead, how Baltimore performs down the stretch could play a factor in how this backfield looks for fantasy managers. With six straight losses, sitting at 4-7, the Ravens aren't entirely out of the playoff picture. They still have four division games left (two against the Steelers). But a few more losses could sink Baltimore and that could lead to less work for Henry and more for Hill. We recommended Hill in the early waiver piece going into Week 12.

Henry is still an RB2 for fantasy but there's also the Week 13 bye — not ideal. Hill has shown he can be an RB3/flex with upside. If you have Henry, you need Hill on your bench. If you're looking for a potential league-winner late in the season, Hill has that upside if the chips fall right.

Kamara can't keep getting away with this, can he?

Last week, it was a tilting five touches for 14 total yards and two scores. This week, it's just TWO yards on two touches, but another touchdown. Seven other carries went to various skill position players and QB Tyler Shough. But at least it was a decent showing by Etienne in his second game back after being placed on injured reserve after Week 3.

It wasn't a dominant performance by Etienne but it was good enough for his managers to trust him back in their lineups. Most of his 76 yards came on a 46-yard run, but that's fine; we wanted to see Etienne get back to making big plays, and that was his biggest of the 2026 season. The volume was also a great sign with Audric Estimé a healthy scratch for Week 11; the backfield was all Etienne's.

The larger issue is the Saints offense. It's not performing up to par, like the boat races and shootouts we saw in flashes last season after Shough took over. The O-line isn't great and Shough has regressed a bit. The rest of the fantasy schedule lines up well for points (at CIN, vs. GB, at CAR), which is a plus. But we need to see some progress from Kellen Moore's group overall in order to have faith in Etienne as an RB2.

The back has that potential but he'll need 15-20 touches and a few big plays mixed in. Etienne is going to lose snaps to Kamara and New Orleans likes using the vet in the red zone. This game has us putting Etienne back in the RB2/3 range, while Kamara is only a risky, TD-dependent flex.

#2714. ‘You just offended most, if not all, of Mexico’: Nick Bosa faces criticism after ‘condescending’ comments about Mexican fans

The San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings will meet in Mexico City on Sunday Night Football in a game that could go a long way toward deciding the NFC's No. 1 seed. But ahead of the big matchup, 49ers superstar defensive end Nick Bosa managed to make headlines for all the wrong reasons.

Bosa drew backlash this week when he suggested that fans in Mexico City need to be told when to cheer during the game. Now, longtime 49ers reporter Grant Cohn has offered Bosa some "friendly advice," saying that his comments came across as "condescending" to the host country.

During a press conference this week, Bosa was asked about the atmosphere when the 49ers last played in Mexico City in 2022. He remembered the crowd being loud, but he had a request for the fans this time around.

"Yeah, I kind of want … I think we need some information given to the fans so they know when to cheer," Bosa said, via NBC Sports Bay Area. "Because they just chant the whole time. If we can kind of teach them, no offense to them and their soccer cheering techniques, but if they can cheer when we're on defense, that would be great."

Needless to say, those comments didn't go over well with a lot of people, including plenty of reporters who cover the NFL. Several members of the media were quick to call Bosa out, including Cohn, who said he "was not expecting Nick Bosa to offend the entire country of Mexico before the 49ers even arrive."

On Saturday, Cohn followed up with a two-minute video offering Bosa some advice. He opened by suggesting that Bosa probably didn't mean to offend anyone.

"Nicholas, Nicholas, Nicholas, you've done it again," Cohn said. "You're a man of few words, but when you do talk, you often get yourself in trouble. And I feel like sometimes you're just misunderstood, like this time. Like, now, you just offended most, if not all, of Mexico. The entire country. And I don't think you meant to do that."

Cohn acknowledged that Bosa was likely "just talking ball," but he made it clear that the comments still came off the wrong way.

"But see, it comes across as condescending," Cohn said. "Because they know. They watch football. They know exactly how Americans cheer; they just don't cheer like that because they want to cheer their way. Frankly, it's a lot more fun."

Cohn then offered Bosa a simple rule to follow in the future to avoid these sorts of situations.

"In the future, Nicholas, anytime you're invited somewhere and you're a guest, it's bad form to tell the host what to do. In any walk of life. You're the guest. What you say is, 'It's so nice to be here. Thank you to the entire country of Mexico for being so generous and welcoming. Can't wait to play at Stadium Azteca.' That's all you say. Period!" Cohn said.

"Just like if you were to go to someone's house for dinner. You'd say, 'Hey, man, thank you for dinner and thank you having me.' Not like, 'Yo, turn the heater up to 78 and give me eight ice cubes in my drink. And make it a half-Coke, half-orange soda mixture right now. Actually, I want peanut butter and jelly.' That's what you don't do!" he added.

Clearly, Bosa will have plenty of motivation to get that first sack of the season on Sunday night. It will be interesting to see how the crowd in Mexico City treats him when he does.

- Spurs lose Dylan Harper for 1-3 weeks: Not only did the Spurs' 12-game winning streak end on November 17 against the Pistons, but they also lost a key player. Harper was injured late in the fourth quarter when he slipped while attempting to catch a pass, suffering a hip strain that's expected to sideline him anywhere from one to three weeks.

As has been the case when the Spurs were down another perimeter player this season, Julian Champagnie has returned to the starting lineup. In wins over the Clippers and Pelicans, he totaled 29 points (11-of-24 FGs), seven rebounds, four assists, one block and seven three-pointers. Champagnie stands to be most valuable to fantasy managers needing three-point production.

Also of note from those two games without Harper was Stephon Castle's play. While he committed eight turnovers against the Clippers, the third-year guard totaled 40 points (14-of-24 FGs, 5-of-5 FTs), nine rebounds, 18 assists, four steals, seven three-pointers and 10 turnovers. Although his field-goal percentage has decreased a few points (43.7 compared to 47.1 in 2025-26), Castle has kept the turnovers in check this season, with his average down to 2.4 per game (from 3.2 tpg last season)

- 76ers lose Jaylen Brown (hamstring): After playing 33 minutes in the 76ers' November 16 win over the Nets, Brown was diagnosed with a strained left hamstring that sidelined him for Philadelphia's final two games of Week 5. He was supposed to be re-evaluated ahead of Saturday's game against the Bucks, but the team released no news. Brown, who did some individual work at Friday's practice, is day-to-day until the 76ers provide a firm timeline. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope started the two games Brown missed, recording totals of 19 points (7-of-11 FGs), nine rebounds, three assists, two steals and five three-pointers. The veteran guard is a decent option for deep-league managers needing three-point production, with steals being a bonus.

Also, VJ Edgecombe played 43 and 38 minutes in the two games Philadelphia played without Brown to end Week 5, recording totals of 40 points (13-of-27 FGs, 9-of-9 FTs), 11 rebounds, 12 assists, four steals, one block and five three-pointers. While his shot attempts have increased slightly in Brown's absence, Edgecombe's increased playing time stands out and likely raises the second-year guard's fantasy ceiling in the short term.

- Raptors' injury woes continue as Barrett, CMB go down: Already playing without Kawhi Leonard, whose knee injury has kept him out since October 23, Toronto lost RJ Barrett (hamstring) and Collin Murray-Boyles (concussion protocol) during Week 5. Barrett will be re-evaluated in two weeks, while Murray-Boyles' timeline depends on how soon he's cleared to resume full activity. Those injuries have freed up opportunities for multiple players, including Jamison Battle and first-round pick Allen Graves.

In games against the Wizards and Pistons, Battle totaled 29 points (11-of-21 FGs), 10 rebounds, one steal and seven three-pointers. While he started against Washington and played 33 minutes, Battle was used in a reserve role in the November 20 win over Detroit, playing 20 minutes. As for Graves, he had a career night against Detroit, finishing with 20 points (6-of-9 FGs, 6-of-6 FTs), 10 rebounds, one assist, three steals, one block and two three-pointers. While he came off the bench for his lone season at Santa Clara, Graves' advanced numbers were a big reason he was selected in the first round. Like Murray-Boyles, he has the tools needed to be a reliable category-league option for fantasy managers.

- Anthony Edwards (knee) reveals that he has no return timeline: Sidelined since the final week of October after undergoing an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee, Edwards met with the media ahead of the Timberwolves' November 19 loss to the Knicks. The Timberwolves star said he doesn't have a firm return timeline, so it could go longer than the initially reported two-month timeline. Ayo Dosunmu has been the replacement in the starting lineup, and he's performed well, averaging 19.7 points, 4.5 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.6 steals and 2.4 three-pointers in 13 starts.

Jaden McDaniels is enjoying the best individual season of his NBA career, while LaMelo Ball and Jonathan Kuminga have fit in well with his new team. Since losing Edwards, the Timberwolves have gone 9-4 and looked like a team more than capable of holding down the fort until their star returns. The one concern for Minnesota may be Rudy Gobert, who has continued to struggle offensively. His scoring average of 7.6 points per game is the lowest since his rookie season (2013-14).

- Austin Reaves (heel) should return...but when?: Reaves has missed the Lakers' last four games with a left heel contusion, but he could be back "soon." Ahead of Friday's win over the Kings, Lakers head coach JJ Redick said that he hoped to get Reaves back within the next two games. If Reaves can't play on Monday against the Jazz, the next possible return day would be the day after Thanksgiving against the Spurs in San Antonio. Quentin Grimes has performed well as the replacement in the starting lineup, hitting 10 three-pointers and dropping 47 points in an overtime win over the Hornets, but the Lakers also need Reaves back to ease some of the pressure on Luka Dončić as a playmaker.

- Stephen Curry (oblique) to be re-evaluated: Injured on November 11, Curry was given a re-evaluation timeline of two weeks, which falls in the middle of Week 6. Obviously, he isn't guaranteed to return to the court immediately, but the Warriors desperately need their star guard back. Not only has Golden State lost all four games that Curry's missed, but they also haven't been competitive. During this five-game losing streak, which began with the game against the Rockets in which Curry was injured, the Warriors have led for a total of 46 seconds and have four wire-to-wire defeats.

While Yaxel Lendeborg has done what he can in Curry's absence, making him the primary scoring option puts him in an incredibly difficult spot. Lendeborg's efficiency has suffered, while Brandin Podziemski has scored 15 points or less in each of the Warriors' last four games.

- Evan Mobley is expected to be re-evaluated: Mobley has been out since the Cavaliers' November 11 win over the Knicks with a toe injury, and on November 16 it was reported that he would be re-evaluated in 7-10 days. Given the timeline, he should be re-evaluated early in Week 6, with Cleveland playing three games next week. They'll play road games against the Bulls (Monday) and Knicks (Wednesday) before hosting the Heat on Sunday. Tyrese Proctor initially moved into the starting lineup after Peyton Watson was sidelined for the November 14 win over the Mavericks, and he's remained in that role since Watson returned.

In four starts, Proctor averaged 13.5 points, 4.0 rebounds, 3.8 assists and 2.3 three-pointers per game, shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 60 percent from the foul line. It should be noted that the first game of that stretch, the win over Dallas, was played without Cleveland's entire starting five. Proctor's production has decreased game by game, but Monday's matchup with the Bulls could be a good one for him.

- Norman Powell (hamstring) to be re-evaluated during Week 6: Powell has been diagnosed with a "mild" strain of his right hamstring and is expected to be re-evaluated during Week 6. The Bulls open their Week 6 at home against the Cavaliers on Monday, so that game can likely be ruled out. Chicago finishes the week with games against the Hornets (Wednesday) and the Pacers (Saturday), so fantasy managers may not get anything out of Powell.

With Isaac Okoro already in the starting lineup due to Caleb Wilson's broken hand, Buddy Hield could be the player who steps in for Powell. The veteran guard has scored in double figures in four of his last five games, and he's made at least two three-pointers in five straight games. Hield doesn't qualify as a must-add player, but he's worth watching in the Bulls' Week 5 finale against the Nuggets on November 22.

- Atlanta, Dallas and Washington have two-game weeks: The Hawks, Mavericks and Wizards play two games in Week 6. However, while Dallas and Washington will each play a game before Thanksgiving, both of Atlanta's games will be played after the holiday. The Hawks have been without Kingston Flemings (back) and CJ McCollum (calf) recently, with the latter not expected to be re-evaluated for another three weeks. Aaron Wiggins has moved into the starting lineup, while the playmaking responsibilities have been shared among Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Dyson Daniels and Jalen Johnson. Hopefully, the time off is enough for Flemings to return if he can't play in Atlanta's Week 5 finale against the Pistons on November 22.

1. Will Jaylen Brown be able to return during Week 6?

#2707. Officials give Jameis Winston a TD, replays appear to show he was down before scoring

The officials gave Giants quarterback Jameis Winston a touchdown on a fourth-and-goal tush push today against the Jaguars, but on replay it’s not at all clear that Winston actually scored.

Winston dove into a mass of bodies, and his helmet appeared to touch the ground before the ball crossed the goal line. The officials signaled touchdown, and play was not stopped for a replay review, but former NFL referee Gene Steratore said on the CBS broadcast that it did not appear to be a touchdown.

There wasn’t a perfect replay angle, and the Jaguars were called for offside on the play, so even if Winston had been ruled short, the Giants would have been given another chance. Still, it does appear that the Giants were given a touchdown they didn’t actually score.

The Giants have a 10-3 lead over the Jaguars at the start of the second quarter.

#2705. Eagles vs. Steelers: The good, the bad, and the ugly

It looks like Nick Sirianni has his job for another week. It looks like the Eagles are heading towards a threepeat as NFC East champions, and another playoff run in 2026.

Well, one of those statements may have a drop of truth to it after the Eagles snapped one streak and preserved another in a 19-16 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on an overcast Sunday at Lincoln Financial Field.

The Eagles snapped their seven-game losing streak, their longest since 2012, during Andy Reid's last season. The Eagles also continued their streak at home against Pittsburgh, winning for the 12th-straight time over the Steelers, who have not won in Philadelphia since October 24, 1965, (20–14 at Franklin Field), 61 years and two stadiums ago.

Maybe the addition of former Eagles' coach T.J. Paganatti as a consultant had something to do with the Eagles' offensive line looking the best it has this season. The defense was strong, holding the Steelers to 73 yards rushing, 43 yards below their season average of 116 yards a game, and sacking 42-year-old relic Aaron Rodgers five times for minus-45 yards.

Joe Milton was competent, moving the Eagles, especially in clutch situations, completing 11 of 21 passes for 141 yards.

Saquon Barkley made a brief appearance as Saquon Barkley rushing for a game-high 75 yards, the bulk of which came on a first quarter 38-yard touchdown run, while Jeremiah Trotter Jr. led the defense with a game-high 13 tackles, Marcus Epps had his best game this season with a season-high 8 tackles, and a bunch of guys who had received very little playing time making significant contributions like Byron Young's two sacks, Jon Jones' three defended passes, and Gabe Hall coming off the practice squad for a sack.

But are they suddenly cured of the slopfest they perpetrated over the first nine games—absolutely not.

If the Eagles can somehow beat Dallas, in Dallas, on Thanksgiving, with the lowly tanking Arizona Cardinals and Indianapolis Colts following them, this nightmare of a season could have life, with the Eagles sitting at 6-7 in an NFC East Division up for grabs.

Did Sunday's victory resuscitate the Eagles or briefly camouflage a bad football team for one week and in the long run hurt its draft status?

The answer may be four days from now in Dallas.

The Eagles are no longer the proud owners of the NFL's current longest losing streak, which has now been handed down I-95 to sinking Baltimore Ravens' six-game skid after starting the season 4-1.

For four days, everything will be right in Eaglesland. Sirianni is 6-0 after the bye week, Milton will no doubt stir comparisons by Eagles' fans and podcasters to Randall Cunningham, and the true believers will begin making their reservations to Los Angeles for mid-February.

There was a pile of good, some bad and smallest amount of ugly this season in the Eagles' 19-16 win over the flailing Pittsburgh Steelers.

Joe Milton's game-clinching third-down, seven-yard completion with less a minute to play to DeVonta Smith.

The Eagles' defense. They kept the Steelers to under 100 yards in the first half. Vic Fangio dialed up blitzes, stunts, and caused all kinds of problems for Aaron Rodgers. They sacked Rodgers five times for minus-45 yards and kept the Steelers out of the end zone for their first 10 drives before Max Hurleman's 20-yard touchdown reception from Aaron Rodgers with 1:21 to play.

Gabe Hall came up from the practice squad to sack Rodgers for the fifth time, taking the old river down for a nine-yard loss on the Steelers' second drive in the fourth quarter. At the time,the Eagles sacked Rodgers five times for minus-45 yards.

Milton had a knack for completing big passes in big situations. His nine-yard completion to Darius Cooper for a first down on a third-and-six on the Eagles' first drive of the fourth quarter was one of them. It was just the second first down for the Eagles in their first five second half possessions. Milton later converted another third down by hitting Cooper for a 14-yard completion on a third-and-10 at the Steelers' 31 on the Eagles' second fourth quarter drive.

Nolan Smith's seven-yard sack on the Steelers' second play of the fourth quarter, zapping Pittsburgh's hopes of tying the game on a third-and-eight at the Eagles' 35. More importantly, the Smith sack pushed the Steelers out of field goal range and forced a punt with 13:12 left to play. The problem was, the Eagles had not moved the ball since the first quarter, only gaining 30 yards since torching the Steelers' defense for 128 yards of total offense in the opening frame.

Safety Marcus Epps had his best game this season, coming up to make tackles for short gains. He stopped Germie Bernard on a second-and-10 in the third quarter, he came up and took down Rico Dowdle for a three-yard loss in the second quarter. He finished with a season-high eight tackles—all solos.

Jake Elliott hitting field goals of 41, 29, 53 and 55 yards. Elliott is 11 of 12 on field goal attempts, and 18 of 18 on extra points. Elliott is 4-for-4 on field goals attempts of 50 yards or more. Hehas quietly had a great season. It makes you wonder why Nick Sirianni kept going for it on fourth down this season on the plus side of the field with Elliott kicking so well.

Braden Mann's 70-yard punt that pinned the Steelers at their four after a three-and-out on the Eagles' second possession of the second half.

Cornerback Jon Jones making a diving deflection on an Aaron Rodgers' pass intended for Roman Wilson at the goal line on the Steelers' second drive of the second quarter. Jones later came up to break up a fourth-quarter attempt to Wilson.

Linebacker Jonathan Greenard's 12-yard sack on the Steelers' first drive of the second quarter on a third-and-19.

Defensive tackle Byron Young's nine-yard on the Steelers' first drive of the second quarter. Young had his second sack late in the third quarter, pulling down old man Rodgers for seven yards on first-and-10.

The first quarter. The Eagles scored a season-high 13 points after they had scored a total of 28 points in their first nine games in the first quarter. They had 128 total yards of offense to Pittsburgh's 35 and five first downs to the Steelers' one. The Eagles' 13-0 lead was their largest this season.

Saquon Barkey's 38-yard sideline touchdown run for a 13-0 first quarter lead. It was classic Barkley, using his considerable speed to run away from TJ Watt trying to catch him from the backside and finding a rare hole.

Milton hitting Cooper with a 29-yard rope down the sideline on a third-and-13 to the Steelers' 28, and Dallas Goedert for a 38-yard pass on a great touch pass on a third-and-18 to the Steelers' 13 on the Eagles' second drive. Unfortunately, the Eagles were only able to get a Jake Elliott field goal out of it.

The Eagles getting the Steelers off the field on Pissburgh's first three drives for a total of 23 yards and no first downs. Of the Steelers' first seven plays, the Eagles had two plays for zero and minus-1 yard, and an average of 2.3 yards a play. The Eagles held the Steelers on fourth-and-one, and had Pittsburgh facing a third-and-eight and third-and-14.

Jihaad Campbell taking down Steelers tailback Jaylen Warren for a one-yard loss on the Steelers' second drive at the Steelers' 21.

Jake Elliott nailed a 41-yard field goal with 10:01 left in the first quarter.

Jeremiah Trotter Jr. slicing through on fourth-and-inches to bring down Warren down for no gain on the Steelers first drive at the Pittsburg 40. It was the utmost disrespect by Steelers' coach Mike McCarthy, thinking he could convert a fourth-down gamble that early in the game. McCarthy practically gave the Eagles a 3-0 lead. The Steelers had far more to lose as a playoff contender than what the hapless Eagles were playing for. In each game Trotter has started, he led the Eagles in tackles, and this game was no different. He made a game-high 13 tackles and led the Eagles again with 9 solo tackles. He continues to prove he is a bonafide NFL starter. Trotter and Campbell actually teamed well together combining for 20 tackles, 14 solo and one tackle for loss.

The Eagles' second quarter. They gained just 13 yards and no first downs in the quarter, while giving up 64 yards and seven first downs.

Milton missing an open DeVonta Smith down the sideline on the Eagles' fourth drive. Milton missed Smith down the middle of the field on the first play of the Eagles' second possession (after a fumble on the second half kickoff).

The Eagles coming away with just two Jake Elliott field goals on their first two drives flagged once and sacked twice for minus-17 yards.

The third quarter. The Eagles picked up only 17 yards and one first down in the quarter. They were 0 for 3 on third-down conversions.

Rookie right tackle Markel Bell and right guard Tyler Steen being split by T.J. Watt for a four-yard loss with 4:06 left in the third quarter. It was typical about everything this season. No one knew who to block Watt, with Bell thinking he was handing Watt off to Steen and Steen thinking Bell had him. Neither had him.Jaydon Blue's fumble on the second half kickoff at the Eagles' 26 was the first really ugly thing that happened. Fortunately, the Eagles' defense bailed him out with a stop that forced a Chris Boswell 40-yard field with 13:55 left in the third quarter.

#2704. Rockets must choose carefully in strange 2027 NBA Draft

If the 2026-27 NBA season ended today, the Houston Rockets would have roughly a 64% chance of landing a top-five pick.

I thought it was roughly 80%. The Brooklyn Nets and Phoenix Suns both have 40%-ish odds; add them together, 40%.

I was, as is so often the case, corrected on X. If each independent event has a 40% chance of happening, each has a 60% chance of not happening. So anyway, long and short, accounting for that, it's about 64%.

Remember when Rafael Stone said not to judge the James Harden trade until 2030? Well, we're almost in 2027, and it feels pretty safe to credit Stone's vision. The Rockets are 12-4; it's nearly certain that they'll have a lottery pick (and probably two) this summer, and there's a pretty good chance one of those picks lands in the top five. Life is good.

There's always a catch, isn't there? The Rockets draft one of the best centers of all time in the same draft that the best player of all time is drafted in. They change NBA offense, but another team changes it even more. Whatever.

The catch is that this draft is widely viewed as weak. If you've researched it, you've likely come to the same conclusion. There's Kansas' Tyran Stokes, and then…yeah.

At least, the list of (nearly) surefire NBA stars begins and ends with Stokes. That doesn't mean there aren't quality players in the draft:

It means Rafael Stone will have to dig for them.

Caveat One: We're early in the draft cycle. It's entirely possible that someone whose name isn't in the most thorough Excel file on the most obsessive aspiring internet scout's laptop.

Caveat Two: I wrote a whole piece about how the Rockets should be looking at Baba Oladotun, and he's averaging a red-hot 4, 2, and 1. Have your grain of salt on hand.

Right now, I'm fixated on two particular prospects. Illinois' Quentin Coleman is a 6'4″ combo guard. I'm convinced he's got a distinctly positive wingspan – I'd estimate 6'8″ – but Google has no idea. He's averaging 17.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, and 4.4 assists while shooting 55.6% from the field and 37.0% from three-point range on 5.4 attempts per game.

The cool thing about Coleman is that he's a lead ball-handler who plays with the energy of a role player. He reminds me of a young Lonzo Ball, with maybe a bit more on-ball juice and a bit less defense.

The other is Ivan Kharchenkov, a 6'7″, 230-pound wing on Arizona. Kharchenkov almost entered the draft last year. He's an outstanding, aggressive perimeter defender with some ancillary skills: He can pass and dribble some. The problem with Kharchenkov has always been his low three-point volume, which never bodes well for an NBA role player.

This year, Kharchenkov is forcing us to ask a question: What if he isn't a role player? He's averaging 22.6 points, 8.0 rebounds, and 4.6 assists per game.

There are concerns about Kharchenkov. He's still shooting just 4.0 threes per game. It's also been suggested that his strength-based shot creation won't work in the NBA, where men are stronger. If he's forced to fend for himself, Kharchenkov tends to muscle into his defender with a few dribbles to create space for his mid-range.

Those are my guys. You may have your own. The broader point is this: Very few "bad" NBA drafts are as bad as they were perceived to be in hindsight. It does happen, but more often, there are stars hiding in plain sight. At this convergence of fortune and strategy, all the Rockets can do is choose carefully. It could be the difference between finding the would-be best team in the NBA's missing piece, and adding another dud to rot away in the 8th man spot until he's trade fodder.

For now, let's wait and see what the Draft Gods decide.

#2703. All six Thanksgiving teams won on Sunday

The Madden movie failed to properly honor the great John Madden. The franchises that will play on Thanksgiving have done their part to make up for it.

All six of the teams that will take the field on the annual day the NFL uses to recognize and remember Madden emerged with wins in the early window on Sunday.

The Lions beat the Bucs, 31-21. The Bears suffocated the Saints, 21-13. The Eagles continued the Steelers’ inability to win in Philly, 19-16. The Cowboys overwhelmed the Titans, 51-30. And the Chiefs and Bills made easy work of the Cardinals and Dolphins, respectively, 34-7 and 26-9.

It sets up a trio of consequential games on Thursday. The 8-2 Bears at the 8-2 Lions could be the most significant early-window Thanksgiving game of all time. The Eagles-Cowboys game has some added sizzle, now that the Cowboys have a chance to get to .500. And the 8-2 Chiefs at the 9-1 Bills should feel like a playoff game.

With all six teams winning on Sunday, everybody wins on Thursday.

And the game between the 6-4 Packers and the 6-4 Rams the night before the tripleheader should be a good one, too. Not to mention the Black Friday game between the likely 8-2 Broncos and the suddenly desperate 6-4 Steelers.

#2701. Is Raiders TE Brock Bowers Playing vs. Broncos?

The Las Vegas Raiders were prepared for the worst when star tight end Brock Bowers had to leave the Week 10 game against the Seattle Seahawks with an ankle injury. While head coach Klint Kubiak called the injury "significant," Bowers was able to practice this week.

The Raiders listed him as questionable, which was a good sign that he could play in Week 11 against the Denver Broncos. Unfortunately, he wasn't able to get ready in time. The Raiders officially listed him as inactive vs. the Broncos.

This is pretty bad news for the Raiders. Bowers is the only player on offense consistently making plays. Without him, it's hard to see how they'll be able to score points against a very good Broncos defense.

Michael Mayer, Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor and Jack Bech really have to step up if the Raiders are going to have any chance.

The team now just has to hope that this is a one-week absence for Bowers. He's already missed two games previously. He's an elite player when he's on the field, but the injury issues are starting to pile up. The Raiders' bye week is coming up, so they may choose to rest him until they get through that.

The Raiders were methodical in how they first decided to play rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza, but there could be some regret. His debut was against the No. 1 defense in the NFL, and it didn't go well.

Now he gets to play another elite defense without his best offensive weapon. The Raiders just need to hope that Mendoza can get out of the game unscathed. It's hard to imagine they'll be able to score very many points against the Broncos. They can't run the ball, and the wide receivers have been terrible.

Now, the Broncos' offense also isn't very good. If the Raiders' defense can have a good game, they'll have a chance to pull off the upset, but it's highly unlikely this game ends up being a shootout.

Mendoza only has one game under his belt, but he gained a lot of fans during his time in college. He may have had an underwhelming debut, but expectations are still very high for him.

Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph has a lot of respect for Mendoza's game.

"He's got the great size, great arm talent, he's athletic, he's smart," Joseph said, via Raiders.com. "He was poised, I mean did not look shook at all. The first half [against Seahawks] was really good, I think once [Brock] Bowers went out, it kind of hurt the game plan a little bit, but the first drive – I mean it's 11 plays, touchdown. And he's making plays with his legs. he's making throws. … But he is poised, and he can make every single throw and it's not too big for him."

Mendoza is going to be seeing the Broncos a lot over the course of his career, so he has to hope he's able to make a strong first impression.

#2697. ANALYSIS: Does Nets’ closing problem have solution?

The idea of having the best of both worlds sounds nice, right?

Unfortunately, in life, things typically don't work that way. There are trade-offs in just about everything. The frustrating part is that either choice feels wrong, especially in the NBA. But neither choice is exactly right, either.

It's an interesting conundrum, especially if you are the 2026-27 Brooklyn Nets.

Through 15 games, Brooklyn, sitting at 3-12, has somehow managed to lose five games by 15+ points. It's the most in the league. However, the squad has also dropped four games by five points or fewer.

That's what makes the Nets' start to the season so interesting. There have certainly been several blowouts, and the squad has only three wins, but there is also a chunk of games where Brooklyn was in it until the final buzzer. That includes Friday's tough 113-111 loss to the Orlando Magic.

According to Cleaning the Glass, Brooklyn has won 1.4 fewer games than their point differential would suggest, the fifth-worst mark in the league. Based on their -7.1 point differential, the Nets would be expected to have 4.4 wins through 15 games.

When those games get tight, the Nets just haven't been able to pull away consistently. Despite having the NBA's highest effective field goal percentage in the fourth quarter, their shooting drops off significantly in clutch situations — the final few minutes of games. The Nets are shooting just 37.2% from the field in those moments, ranking 23rd in the league. Their free-throw shooting has been even worse, sitting at 60%, the fourth-worst mark.

Subsequently, the Nets' winning percentage in clutch situations is just 20.0%, the third-lowest clip in the NBA. The biggest problem comes with closing games, not necessarily being competitive or keeping it close entering the fourth.

Is it coaching? Is it execution? Is it the lack of a closer? The Nets seem to be searching for those same answers themselves.

However, from afar, Jordi Fernández looks to be facing a deeper problem that could be out of control. There is only so much he can do with his rotations. Even on Friday night, he switched up a multitude of components in his minutes distribution, including starting Danny Wolf over Egor Dëmin, which ultimately panned out.

In large part, the overarching issue with Brooklyn comes back to the trade-off element. Want more scoring? There's a good chance you're sacrificing defense. Prioritize the other end? You probably have to sacrifice scoring.

Fernández isn't entirely absolved of blame, but the Nets lack legitimate two-way players. And when you're trying to win a game in the final minutes, particularly against more talented teams, that only makes it harder.

The Nets have been stuck in a tough predicament, trying to balance what matters most in late-game situations: offense or defense. That has cost them in multiple games.

At the end of the day, the Nets don't have an established closing lineup. And that's hard to overcome in today's NBA, especially when games slow down in the final few minutes, and there's little margin for error.

Think about some of the better teams in the league, some that Brooklyn has even played. When a game gets tight, there is a pretty solid understanding of who's getting the basketball. Most solid squads have that guy they trust in crucial situations to turn to when things start to break down.

First off, who is that guy for the Nets? Michael Porter Jr. is probably the closest thing. He has been their most dependable offensive weapon, but is he really that high-end takeover guy?

That's where the roster's lack of two-way versatility becomes even more problematic. When Fernández needs offense, he has to consider which players give Brooklyn the best chance to score. However, in many cases, that comes at the expense of defense. That's what's so frustrating with the state of the roster.

Unfortunately for the Nets, it's not as simple as just putting "the five best players" out on the court. It's simply not how the roster is constructed: eight players are on rookie contracts, and the team is the second-youngest in the NBA over the past 25 years, older than only last year's group.

The Nets lack a proven guy who can dominate games down the stretch. Obviously that comes over time, and for a rebuilding team like Brooklyn, a player like that doesn't emerge overnight. The hope is that Mikel Brown Jr. can become that guy, and the early returns on the rookie are promising so far, but he is still just 12 games into his NBA career while also being on a minutes restriction.

Individually, Brooklyn has pieces that can be useful. It's been promising to see growth from players like Nolan Traoré and Danny Wolf, looking to take legitimate second-year leaps. Julius Randle and MPJ add veteran experience and scoring punch. Then there is someone like Day'Ron Sharpe who has impressed while emerging as the team's starting big.

Those players can be useful. Collectively, though, it's tough to find a five-man combination that doesn't leave something to be desired.

For a young team, there is some encouragement in being competitive. Hanging with high-level teams down the stretch like the Boston Celtics and the New York Knicks is encouraging, but when will those tight games actually translate into wins? There is also a distinction between being competitive but losing and losing games that are supposed to be wins, especially against strong competition. The latter can't always be used as an excuse.

The head coach isn't completely out of this conversation. A few of his rotational decisions, even with the newer changes, have been questionable. Look no further than Noah Clowney.

Clowney, 22, is in the final year of his rookie contract. While he's still 22, he hasn't produced much consistently. That's been the biggest concern with the Alabama product since he entered the league.

Through 15 games, though, he hasn't done much to change that narrative. In 21 minutes per game, he is averaging 6.5 points, 4.2 rebounds, and 1.1 assists on 41.3% from the field.

Furthermore, he owns a team-low -107 plus/minus. For context, that's also a 17-percentage-point difference between him and the second-lowest-rated net: Mo Wagner at -90. Meanwhile, his 3-point percentage (27.7%) is also the lowest on the team among qualified shooters (minimum 3.0 attempts per game).

There have been some glimpses. He had back-to-back games against Memphis and New Orleans where he finished with at least 15 points and two 3s. Overall, though, not much has changed. The flashes are still there, but Clowney continues to struggle to find that level of consistency.

And that brings us back to Friday night, when he finished with zero points in 22 minutes, shooting 0-of-4 from the field, and recording a team-worst minus-12 rating. Yet, with the game on the line, he was still on the floor, defending Franz Wagner, who hit the game-winning shot over him.

Now Wagner had a tremendous game, finishing with 35 points, and his offensive ability is highly touted. However, putting Clowney out there in that situation was questionable to begin with.

If he isn't providing offensively, what exactly is the team gaining by keeping him out there? While he came away with a block and a steal, he hasn't been regarded as a plus defender, especially for his position and size, at 6'10" and 210 pounds. Most glaringly, his plus/minus rating was not only the lowest on Friday, but it's also the lowest among the whole team this year, and by a pretty wide margin.

Despite that, though, he continues to earn consistent minutes. He ranks eighth on the team in minutes per game (21.0), behind Randle (33.1), Porter (32.9), Dëmin (24.0), Sharpe (23.9), Wolf (23.0), Brown (22.9), and Traoré (22.3). So esentially, he's been the Nets' third player off the bench this season. That's a pretty important role.

Clearly, with him in that role and out on the court to close games, things haven't been working too well. That's where Fernández comes in. He needs to be willing to make more on-the-fly adjustments to the rotation, especially when things aren't working.

How about looking at players like Josh Minott and Drake Powell? Neither has received notable minutes this season out of garbage time. Neither is a proven NBA defender, but is it time to give them minutes to see what happens? It's worked with Danny Wolf.

After all, isn't that supposed to be part of a rebuilding season? Minott, 23, shot 39.5% from deep wth Brooklyn last year after being acquired at the trade deadline, and the organization saw enough to award him a two-year, $9 million extension in the offseason. At 6'8" and 205 pounds, he also has the tools to be a disruptor on the defensive end.

Powell, meanwhile, has spent much of the season in the G League so far with Brooklyn's affiliate, the Long Island Nets. He has played in five NBA games and was called up for Friday, although most of his minutes have come in garbage time. The North Carolina product boasts a 43-inch vertical and a 7-foot wingspan, giving him intriguing potential on offense and defense, notably at the point of attack. That was on display at points last year. In fact, his 91.9 defensive rating led the NBA last December, and the Nets actually went 7-4 that month.

Of course, the Nets have a free agency decision on Clowney coming up in the Summer. And of course, the Nets are bringing Powell along slowly. He was, after all, the biggest reach of the Flatbush 5. But, of course, the offense remains a work in progress. He shot just 28% from 3 during his rookie campaign and a painful 4-of-16 from that range in Summer League, including a 0-of-14 start.

There is also two-way forward Chaney Johnson, who played a firm role in the rotation at the start of the season, but his minutes have gradually disappeared. Johnson still lacks an established offensive game, but he can guard multiple positions on both ends of the floor.

Maybe Minott struggles. Maybe Powell shows that he isn't ready. Maybe Johnson doesn't improve much either. However, getting that understanding is important, especially when things aren't working.

And if one of them does emerge as a useful piece, particularly defensively, that would be huge for the roster's current outlook.

There may not be a perfect solution. At 3-12, though, the team needs to keep experimenting, especially off the bench. Fernández' decision regarding Dëmin and Wolf on Friday paid off; now it's important to see that same mindset carry over to bench minutes.

Given the organization's overall situation, there's much more to gain from trying something different than sticking with what hasn't worked.

#2696. Byron Young delivers two sacks in Eagles’ first game without Jordan Davis

The Eagles traded Jordan Davis during their bye week and got an immediate look at what their remaining defensive tackles could do. Byron Young gave them two sacks in a 19-16 win over Pittsburgh, and Gabe Hall added another.

Young finished with four tackles, two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits. His first sack went for a 9-yard loss and was his first of the season. Young and Hall accounted for three of Philadelphia's five sacks, helping hold Aaron Rodgers to 182 net passing yards despite 44 attempts.

Philadelphia claimed Young off waivers from the Raiders before the 2024 season. His opportunity grew after the Eagles moved Davis to Jacksonville, and Sunday gave the coaching staff a reason to keep him involved. With Jalen Carter and Moro Ojomo also in the interior rotation, the Eagles can use Young in spots where he can get upfield and disrupt the pocket.

Dallas will give the group a different test on Thanksgiving. The Eagles' interior rush has to affect Dak Prescott without opening escape lanes or relying on extra rushers, especially if Philadelphia is thin at outside corner. Young's two sacks earned attention Sunday. His ability to contribute on early downs and give the Eagles another dependable interior rusher will determine how much of the rotation he keeps.

#2688. Game Preview: Knicks vs Pacers, November 22, 2026

Over the last few years, the Pacers have given the Knicks fits.

We all know about the recent postseason history between these two teams, although we won't go into that. Even with Tyrese Haliburton out last season, they battled and made the Knicks work. Outside of the March 17th game in which the Knicks won handily 136-110, the other three games were all close games. Despite being in the middle of a retooling and tanking season, they tried their hardest to beat the Knicks, and even succeeded in doing so once, handing them a 137-134 overtime loss in early February. It also isn't that long ago that the Knicks suffered what is probably the most frustrating loss of their season. Less than 24 hours after the Knicks' most exhilarating win of the season though, they get a chance to get some sweet revenge on an opponent is starting to become way too familiar.

The Pacers enter Sunday's contest 5-11 and are losers of three straight. Haliburton remains sidelined with a hamstring injury, T.J. McConnell is out also with a hamstring injury, and Pascal Siakam is currently listed as a questionable with a hip injury. But given their recent tendency to bring out their big guns for the Knicks, I'd expect Siakam to play. And given their recent ability to test the Knicks even without their starting point guard, I'd expect the Pacers to push the Knicks.

That is unfortunately even more the case considering the situation the Knicks find themselves in. They just played in a game that came down to the last shot and saw Jalen Brunson, Josh Hart, and Landry Shamet all play 35 or more minutes. They are also at risk of being without both Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby for a second straight game due to illness and calf tightness, respectively. We already saw Brunson stretched thin last night against a tough Trail Blazers defense. Having to go without the team's second and third-best offensive players against a Pacers team that tends to defend him tough on the second night of a back-to-back sounds like a pretty tough and unenviable task.

That being said, the Knicks should win this one. I know that was the case against the Pacers the last time they met up, but the Knicks are the better team. Being without Towns and Anunoby hurts them a tremendous amount on both sides of the ball. And that was evident in the final three quarters of last night's game, where we saw the Knicks' offense slowly revert to a heliocentric Brunson iso-fest. The defense held up, partly due to the Trail Blazers offense shooting themselves in the foot, but having Anunoby there obviously helps. And if Siakam is a go tonight, the rosters on paper match up more closely because I don't see who on this roster has the size to really slow him down if Anunoby is out again.

If Bridges continues playing the way he has as of late and Shamet continues to look like prime Stephen Curry reincarnated, it might not matter, though. Brunson will get a lot of shots, and he may not be the most efficient against what should be a very physical Pacers team that has gotten to know Brunson and his endless counter moves pretty well. But he's also been shooting the ball well, especially from three. And he's made everybody quickly forget that slow shooting start he's gotten off to.

When these two teams last met up on November 13th, Jordan Clarkson, Miles McBride, and the aforementioned Shamet combined to go just 5-16 for 14 points while Aaron Nesmith went for 18 points on 7-10 shooting by himself and the supporting cast of Obi Toppin, Jay Huff, Larry Nance, and Quenton Jackson went 9-17 for 22 points. Nesmith has struggled mightily from three over the last few games, in large part due to a hand sprain, hamstring injury, and knee soreness that have reportedly been bothering him. He's currently shooting a career-worst 25% on catch-and-shoot threes, is shooting just 27.4% from three overall this season, and just 22.7% from three in his last 10 games. Nesmith is a pivotal part of the Pacers team, but he's been hurting their offense recently by not even looking to shoot-something the Knicks' very own Hart has done at times as well.

With Brunson and Shamet likely getting a lot of attention and the Pacers needing as much offense as they can get with Haliburton out and Siakam's availability being in question, the game could come down to which group of role players can do more. Can Kelly Oubre, who went for 16 points when these two teams last met, repeat his performance? How about Bridges, who not only hit the game-winning shot last night but scored 18 points against the Pacers not too long ago? And how about the matchup between two glue guys in Hart and Nesmith, both of whom have struggled to score the ball effectively recently?

I expect the Knicks to win this game. But I said that for their last meeting as well. With both sides missing key players, it'll likely be a slugfest. Don't expect an aesthetically pleasing, or even an entertaining game. The Pacers aren't afraid to play that way, and as we've seen, neither are the Knicks. Not that it's necessarily mattered in the past, but the Knicks are trending in the right direction and the Pacers aren't. New York takes this 103-95.

Who: Indiana Pacers (5-11) at New York Knicks (10-6)Date: Sunday, November 22, 2026Time: 8:00 PM ETPlace: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYTV: MSG, NBA TVFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

#2687. Cade Cunningham has just 5 points in Pistons' ugly loss to Hawks

ATLANTA – A late collapsed cost the Detroit Pistons on the road.

They fell to the Atlanta Hawks at State Farm Arena, 107-97, after giving up an 18-0 run to open the fourth quarter. It took more than seven minutes for the Pistons to score a point in the final quarter, and the Hawks turned an 11-point Pistons lead into a seven-point deficit, 92-85, with 6:39 remaining in the game.

Their first points weren't scored until the 4:52 mark, missing seven in a row before Isaiah Joe knocked down a 3-pointer to cut Atlanta's lead back to four. The Pistons lost the offensive glass, 24-8, and were destroyed 27-6 in second chance points.

The Pistons couldn't overcome a poor game from Cade Cunningham, who finished with five points, 15 assists and four rebounds. They were led in scoring by Joe (19 points). Ausar Thompson added 18 points, 11 rebounds, five assists and two blocks, and Collins also scored 18.

After going scoreless in the first half, Cunningham made his first bucket of the night – a midrange jumper – with 10:46 to play in the third quarter. His next bucket wasn't until the game was nearly over, draining a 3-pointer with 36 seconds left.

It was the first time this season Cunningham failed to score at least 10 points, and he shot just 2-for-9 overall. Foul trouble limited him early, as he picked up his third early in the second quarter. But he mostly was content to conduct the action – his 15 assists were a season-high.

SANKOFA: 2006 WNBA champs Shock 'an embodiment of what Detroit truly is'

In the first half, the Pistons were out-rebounded on the offensive glass, 13-4, with a 13-0 disparity in second chance points. Poor work on the boards coast the Pistons during the Hawks' 18-0 run as well, as they gave up four offensive rebounds and seven second-chance points during the run.

A strength for the Pistons last season has become a weakness. John Collins and Paul Reed have been unable to provide the physical, consistent rebounding presence in the paint that they are accustomed to with Jalen Duren. Beyond the cold stretch in the fourth quarter, the Pistons also were unable to win the possession game.

#2683. Broncos, TV legend Tom Jackson dies at 75

Tom Jackson, a 14-year veteran with the Broncos and a longtime fixture on ESPN’s NFL programming, has died. He was 75.

Jackson was a fourth-round pick of the Broncos in 1973. He became a full-time starter in his second season. He started a run of three straight Pro Bowl berths in 1977, the same year the Broncos made their first Super Bowl appearance.

Jackson played until 1986. The next year, he debuted on ESPN. He worked on the network’s Sunday NFL Countdown show and the must-see NFL Primetime, which featured extended highlights packages years before the best plays could be instantly seen on social media.

“All of us are stunned,” Jackson’s long-time on-air partner, Chris Berman, said in a statement. “I’m stunned, we’re stunned and you’re stunned. We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years, primarily on NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown. It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week.”

Jackson is a member of the Broncos’ Ring of Fame, the franchise’s 50th anniversary team, and the Louisville Ring of Honor. He received the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Hall of Fame in 2015.

The recent changes to the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s rules could make Jackson a candidate for the expanded “contributor” category, given that it allows former players to enhance their standing with other contributions to the game. Few have combined an impactful and prolonged playing career with an impactful and prolonged broadcasting career.

We extend our condolences to Jackson’s friends, family, teammates, and colleagues.

#2679. Kings reportedly signing veteran Gabe Vincent to be backup point guard

This had been rumored for weeks. Veteran point guard Gabe Vincent had worked out for the Sacramento Kings and had talked with them about coming in as their backup to rookie Darius Acuff Jr., he reportedly even had a standing offer.

Now, it's finally happening, a story broken by Shams Charania of ESPN and confirmed by other reports.

Vincent, 30, is signing for a veteran minimum contract, and the Kings had an open roster spot, so no other move is needed. Vincent was invited to Knicks training camp to compete for a roster spot, and reportedly also had conversations with Atlanta before the season, but chose not to join either team.

This is a full-circle moment for Vincent, who was born in Modesto (about 75 miles from Sacramento) and played his high school ball in Stockton, about 45 miles away from the Golden One Center where the Kings play. He went on to play his college ball at UC Santa Barbara.

The Kings have been seven points per 100 possessions worse this season with Acuff off the court, they needed a veteran backup point guard after losing Ben Simmons to an Achilles tear before the season. Vincent is being brought in both to stabilize the second unit and to mentor Acuff. Vincent, a seven-year NBA veteran, fills that role. Vincent isn't an elite scorer or shooter (he has averaged 6.7 points per game over his career and is shooting under 40%), but he understands how to play off talented teammates and could work well with Kings such as Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine.

#2678. Broncos lead Raiders 17-10 at halftime

The Broncos got out to a 17-0 lead, but the Raiders have settled in after a rough start to narrow that advantage to 17-10 at halftime.

#2677. Michigan’s Savion Hiter Decision Changes Things Before Ohio State

EUGENE, OREGON - NOVEMBER 14: Quarterback Bryce Underwood #19 of the Michigan Wolverines hands off the ball to Savion Hiter #5 during the first half of the game against the Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Ali Gradischer/Getty Images)

ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 24: Savion Hiter #5 of the Michigan Wolverines plays against the Indiana Hoosiers at Michigan Stadium on October 24, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

The Michigan Wolverines earned a huge recruiting win when they landed Savion Hiter. He was viewed as the No. 1 running back in his class.

He enrolled in January and is now playing his true freshman fall with Michigan — and heading into the Wolverines' game against Ohio State, Hiter is finding his stride.

It's the kind of team-changing development that gives Michigan hope of beating the Buckeyes.

Hiter's talent has never been in question, and in the last two weeks, he has found his stride.

GettyEUGENE, OREGON – NOVEMBER 14: Quarterback Bryce Underwood #19 of the Michigan Wolverines hands off the ball to Savion Hiter #5 during the first half of the game against the Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Ali Gradischer/Getty Images)

Michigan chose over the last couple of weeks to really lean into Hiter, and it's working.

In the loss to Oregon, it didn't matter on the scoreboard — but Hiter had 13 carries for 107 yards.

And then in Saturday's upset over UCLA, it was all Hiter.

They gave Hiter 26 carries and he ran for 104 yards. It wasn't a huge yard per carry total, but it's clear that Michigan was fully committed to this being Hiter's backfield.

It was always going to happen at some point, and it appears that now is that time.

The Wolverines have earned bowl eligibility, so Hiter has a couple games left.

First up is his first edition of The Game against Ohio State.

GettyANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN – OCTOBER 24: Savion Hiter #5 of the Michigan Wolverines plays against the Indiana Hoosiers at Michigan Stadium on October 24, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

Ohio State's offense isn't great right now, but Michigan's seems worse.

Both teams have good defenses, so they'll have to look for subtle edges.

Hiter might be the edge that Michigan can find right now that didn't exist earlier in the season.

Ohio State has had freshmen running backs impact this rivalry clash in the past. This time around, if Michigan is going to hang around, it's likely in part because they find a way to move the chains with Hiter.

That's easier said than done, but keep an eye on the true freshman RB for Michigan on Saturday in Columbus.

#2676. MLB rumors: Rangers in mix for Sato, Dodgers seek infield help, Korean slugger could join free agent class

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with only one significant transaction: Evan Phillips signed with the Braves. Phillips, our 34th-ranked free agent, received a three-year deal worth $35 million. He'll replace Raisel Iglesias in Atlanta's bullpen and pair with Robert Suarez at the end of the game. The Braves could still re-sign Iglesias too, I suppose.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors -- A LOT of rumors -- and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The Rangers are among the teams with interest in Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports The Athletic. Sato primarily played third base for the Hanshin Tigers, though he does not stand out defensively, and could land at first base or in the corner outfield in MLB. Texas could stand to upgrade at first base and could always slot Sato in at DH as well.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available and the best free agent position player. The reigning Triple Crown winner in Japan hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. Sato, 28 in March, has some similarities to Munetaka Murakami as a lefty with big power and swing-and-miss concerns, though Sato is a much more aggressive hitter and won't walk as much as Murakami.

With Miguel Rojas retired, the Dodgers are looking to add a right-handed hitting infielder, according to The Athletic. Mookie Betts and Max Muncy are entrenched on the left side of the infield. Tommy Edman, a switch-hitter, is penciled in at second base, with fellow switch-hitter Alex Freeland next in line as depth. Freeland has not hit much in his limited MLB time, however.

This is not a great free agent class overall, but it does feature several utility infielders who hit right-handed. Among them are Mauricio Dubón, Ha-Seong Kim, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Edmundo Sosa. Glovemen Oswald Peraza (Angels) and Jared Triolo (Pirates) are potential trade targets. Rojas was a very productive role player for Los Angeles. He won't be so easy to replace.

The Padres are receiving calls about catchers Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Top prospect Ethan Salas was called up in September and became the youngest catcher to appear in the postseason in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. Salas is the future behind the plate, making Campusano or Fermin (or perhaps both) expendable.

Campusano and Fermin are very different players. Campusano is a bat-first catcher who might be worth keeping given his age (28) and the fact that the Padres could slot him at DH. That said, those same qualities make him appealing to other teams. Fermin, 31, is a terrific defender who hasn't hit much the last few years. The Padres need pitching and could deal a catcher or two for an arm or two.

Samsung Lions outfielder Ja-Wook Koo has hired a new agent and is looking to make the jump to MLB, reports MLB.com. Koo, a 10-time All-Star and this year's Korean Series MVP, has been among the best hitters in the Korea Baseball Organization the last few years. The 33-year-old hit .371/.458/.581 with 15 homers and nearly as many walks (66) as strikeouts (71) in 2026.

Koo's age and the fact he's a left-handed hitter in a market inundated with left-handed hitting outfielders will work against him in free agency. He has a great track record in Korea, though, including a history of high contact rates, which could make him a cheaper and more appealing target than MLB free agents like Michael Conforto, Trent Grisham, Cedric Mullins, and Daulton Varsho.

Steelers receiver DK Metcalf had an unfortunate stat line on Sunday.

One catch, two yards, two personal fouls, one ejection.

#2674. Taylor Swift Celebrates Travis Kelce’s Second Touchdown With a Very Special Young Chiefs Fan

Taylor Swift had a special young fan by her side as she celebrated her husband Travis Kelce's second touchdown during the Kansas City Chiefs' Week 11 matchup against the Arizona Cardinals.

The 36-year-old singer was watching from a suite at Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday, November 22, when Kelce caught a 22-yard touchdown pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the second quarter.

Cameras captured Swift celebrating the score by hugging her niece, Wyatt Kelce, the eldest daughter of Jason and Kylie Kelce.

Swift was also joined by Kylie and her parents, Andrea and Scott Swift, for the game.

Kelce, 37, had already scored on an 8-yard touchdown reception during Kansas City's opening drive, although the broadcast did not show Swift's reaction to his first score.

The second touchdown gave the Chiefs tight end his first multi-touchdown game of the season.

Swift attended the game wearing a black-and-red Chiefs jacket, large hoop earrings, and burgundy-colored nails.

Her parents also wore Kansas City gear, while Kylie stuck with her longtime tradition of not wearing another NFL team's merchandise.

The Philadelphia Eagles fan wore a gray sweater while holding her youngest daughter, Finn.

Kylie, 34, is married to Travis' older brother, former Eagles center Jason Kelce. The couple shares four daughters: Wyatt, 6, Elliotte, 5, Bennett, 3, and Finn, 1.

Swift has grown close to the Kelce family since she began dating Travis in 2023.

The couple married on July 3, 2026, after nearly three years together.

During the September 16 episode of their "New Heights" podcast, Travis and Jason shared a story about how the girls initially addressed Swift.

While discussing an interaction with actor Tom Cruise, Travis recalled that his nieces had a similar experience when they first met their future aunt.

"We had to break that habit with the girls. When they had to meet Aunt Tay Tay, they were calling her 'Taylor Swift,'" Travis said.

Jason laughed while imitating his daughters.

"'Taylor Swift, can I do this? Taylor Swift?'" he recalled.

Travis called the habit "adorable," while Jason said he eventually told the girls they could simply "call her Taylor."

The November 22 game gave Swift another opportunity to cheer alongside the family as Travis reached a milestone of his own.

The matchup marked his 100th game at Arrowhead Stadium, making him just the fourth player in Chiefs history to reach that mark.

The singer has continued attending Kansas City's home games throughout the 2026 NFL season.

She previously watched the Chiefs play on November 8, when she was joined by longtime friend Karlie Kloss and her parents.

Swift also attended the October 18 game against the Los Angeles Chargers, sitting alongside Este Haim and Caitlin Clark.

Earlier in the season, she made headlines during Kansas City's September 20 victory over the Indianapolis Colts.

After Travis scored his first touchdown of the season, Swift pointed to her wedding ring and shouted, "That's my husband!"

Swift has also attended home games against the Denver Broncos, including the September 14 matchup where she was spotted alongside Cruise.

#2672. Could Tarik Skubal take a short-term, high-AAV contract? Breaking down pros and cons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The expectation is left-hander and two-time AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent available this offseason, will sign a record contract before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are almost certain to lock out the players at that time. Skubal is expected to sign before then.

Skubal, 30 later this month, is a Scott Boras client and Boras tends to shatter records, not beat them narrowly. There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:

Something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

With that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a new contract to stay with his team.

1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a new salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the big picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.

Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander has issued a statement regarding his recent anti-Muslim social media posts that he has since deleted. Santander's statement, which he posted to Instagram and follows a public condemnation of the posts by Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins, reads as follows:

"After taking time to reflect on my recent social media posts and speaking with people I trust and respect, I recognize that I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared on my platform.

"I realize that this content caused hurt and I sincerely apologize. I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared, recognizing the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

"As a man of faith, it is my belief that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their religion, background, or beliefs. After hearing feedback from those I hurt, I realize that the content I shared fell short of my own convictions.

"I would like to affirm my respect for the Muslim community and for the dignity and freedom of people of every faith and background.

"From this experience, I have learned to ensure that none of my communications promote hate or give the impression that I support hatred, discrimination, or violence against anyone."

The club had earlier released a statement on the incident that read:

"Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

Santander, a Venezuela native, shared social media videos following the recent U.S. midterm elections, including one in which a Christian pastor said, "There is no such thing as kind Muslims." Another suggested that Sharia law would be imposed in the U.S. following the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate representing the state of Michigan.

Atkins told reporters Tuesday that Santander's behavior "did not align" with organizational values and there were no words "to express my level of disappointment."

"I talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant," Atkins said. "We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. It's a part of our organizational values and his behavior did not align with that."

Santander, 32, joined the Blue Jays prior to the 2025 season on a five-year, $92.5 million free-agent contract. He struggled badly across 54 games in 2025 and missed the entire 2026 season with injury.

#2670. Fernando Mendoza throws first NFL TD pass on perfect strike to Ashton Jeanty

For the first time in his NFL career, Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza has thrown a touchdown pass.

Mendoza's first NFL touchdown pass came in the second quarter of his second career start, which came in Week 11 of the 2026 season against the Denver Broncos.

On the play, Mendoza dropped back to pass and was given plenty of time to scan the field at the top of his drop. The 23-year-old rookie then saw running back Ashton Jeanty break open on the sideline, earning a couple of yards of separation against Broncos linebacker Que Robinson.

Jeanty was able to catch Mendoza's perfectly-thrown ball in stride. He then kept his feet after Robinson attempted to trip him up and scampered into the end-zone for a 68-yard score.

While Mendoza's strike to Jeanty was his first career passing touchdown, it was the second of his brief NFL career to date. The rookie logged a 10-yard rushing touchdown in his first start, a 21-13 Week 10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

Mendoza expressed in a post to LinkedIn, his only social media platform, he had improvements to make after being promoted into the starter role.

"A lot to learn from my first NFL start," Mendoza wrote. "Grateful for my family, friends, and Raider Nation for the support! Looking forward to getting better and earning the trust of my teammates and coaches every day.

Mendoza's early performance against the Broncos would suggest he is already making some strides as he develops on the fly. He completed 6 of 13 passes for 127 yards and a touchdown in the first half against the Broncos, though he was sacked three times for a loss of 27 yards.
